summary: Documents a process for organizing future development of SIP and related work in the Real-time Applications and Infrastructure area. It aims to keep changes and extensions coordinated as SIP is used in more environments. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: SIP is used in many places, and everyone wants to change it. This document sets the rules for how changes are proposed and approved so it does not turn messy.

subtitle: How SIP and other real-time work in the IETF gets proposed, filtered and approved, and why the old "P-" header route was dropped.

tldr.problem: SIP became popular far beyond its origins, which brought a flood of proposed changes and extensions that could threaten interoperability and security. The earlier change process, RFC 3427, had limits, especially its "P-" header fields.
tldr.mechanism: Two long-lived working groups split the job: SIPCORE maintains the core SIP specifications, and DISPATCH decides where new work in the RAI Area belongs. Informational header fields go through Designated Expert review instead of the "P-" route.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3427 and is a Best Current Practice (BCP 67). It has since been updated by RFC 7957.

today: RFC 5727 is a Best Current Practice that obsoletes RFC 3427. It is listed as updated by RFC 7957 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a New Change Process
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP, RFC 3261) grew well beyond Internet multimedia sessions and became popular for Voice-over-IP and IP telephony. The result was a continual flood of proposals to modify and extend it. The challenge for the IETF was to keep baseline interoperability across many implementations.

The earlier answer was RFC 3427, which gave the SIP and SIPPING working groups a guardian role and let outside groups define limited-use extensions through "P-" header fields. Over time that structure showed limits, and this document obsoletes it with a new structure for the Real-time Applications and Infrastructure (RAI) Area.
sections.eli5: SIP got so popular that everyone wanted to add their own rules. The old rulebook did not work well any more, so a new one was written.

sections.title: SIPCORE and DISPATCH
sections.content:
The SIPCORE working group takes over the role of the old SIP working group. It must handle every document that updates or obsoletes RFCs 3261 through 3265 or their successors. All SIP extensions considered there must be Standards Track. Its charter is open-ended so it can remain the place for core SIP development.

The DISPATCH working group replaces SIPPING and covers the whole RAI Area, not just SIP. It does not take on specifications itself. Instead it finds the right venue for new work and, if none exists, develops charters and consensus for a BoF, working group or exploratory group. A DISPATCH review is not required before a proposed change to core SIP goes to SIPCORE, but work that does not clearly fit an existing RAI effort should be examined by DISPATCH.

DISPATCH may conclude one of four things: the requirements justify a change to core SIP and belong in SIPCORE; they need a new effort in RAI; they fall within existing chartered work; or the proposal should not be acted on now. It is also meant to filter out uses of SIP "just because it is there", such as controlling household appliances.
sections.eli5: One group looks after the main rulebook. Another group is like a front desk that sends each new idea to the right team, or says not now.

sections.title: Introducing New Work to RAI
sections.content:
Proposals are best written as individual Internet-Drafts. The RFC advises writing a problem statement first, or at least separately from the protocol mechanism, because that speeds up consensus. A problem statement should explain what needs solving, why existing mechanisms are insufficient, why SIP is the right solution if SIP is to be modified, and any security issues that result.

DISPATCH chairs and the RAI Area Directors decide whether the problem is outside existing charters. If so, the DISPATCH deliverable may be a problem statement draft, a charter or similar, but it must not include protocol development. Once the IESG, with IAB advice, approves the new charter or BoF, DISPATCH has finished its job and the new effort becomes autonomous.

DISPATCH is not the only entry point. Working groups that already have chartered deliverables, and Area Directors who accept charter revisions, are unaffected. SIPCORE itself must protect the architectural integrity of SIP: it must not add features without general use, and must not add features just for efficiency at the expense of simplicity or robustness.
sections.eli5: If you have a new idea, first explain the problem you want to fix. Only then do people look at your fix.

sections.title: Extensibility and the End of "P-" Headers
sections.content:
The old "P-" prefix stood for "preliminary", "private" or "proprietary". It was meant to keep such header fields in closed environments, but it did not work: some "P-" fields, such as P-Asserted-Identity, were widely implemented, and the prefix left no plausible migration path to general use.

This document therefore deprecates the RFC 3427 guidance on creating "P-" header fields. Existing ones are still handled as their specifications say, so there is no change in protocol behavior. New experimental or private header fields should not use the prefix, and using any such prefix ("P-", "X-" and so on) is discouraged. Instead they may be registered through Informational RFCs or outside documents under Designated Expert review.

The expert must check two criteria. The header field MUST be purely informational and MUST NOT significantly change the behavior of SIP entities. It also MUST NOT undermine SIP security, and its draft must address security in detail as if it were Standards Track.

The deprecation does not change how SIP methods, URI parameters, response codes or option tags are registered.
sections.eli5: A "for testing only" sticker on a header did not stop people from using it everywhere. So the sticker is retired, and a reviewer checks new headers instead.

sections.title: SIP Event Packages
sections.content:
RFC 3265 defines normal event packages and event template-packages. Template-packages can only be created through a Standards Track RFC from an IETF working group. For normal packages, this document replaces the old "First Come First Serve" registration policy.

A package developed outside a working group must first be published as an Internet-Draft for review by DISPATCH. It is then registered under the "RFC Required" policy together with a Designated Expert. Among the rules, the package MUST NOT define a template-package, MUST NOT overlap chartered packages, MUST NOT contradict SIP or SIP events, and MUST NOT undermine security. It must be documented in an individual Informational RFC and may need an applicability statement explaining why it is not for general SIP use.
sections.eli5: Adding a new kind of SIP announcement used to be first come, first served. Now someone checks that it does not clash with existing ones.

sections.title: Registries and Summary
sections.content:
Method names, option tags and response codes still require a Standards Action. Informational registration of header fields that do not start with "P-" is now permitted if a Designated Expert approves. Standard header fields and messages MUST NOT begin with "P-", and short forms of header fields MUST only go to Standards Track header fields. Event template-packages need a Standards Action within an IETF working group.

A clarification in section 7.1 settles a contradiction in RFC 3969: registering new SIP URI parameters requires Standards Action.

The RFC's own summary is three lines. Documents updating or obsoleting RFCs 3261 through 3265 go through SIPCORE. Other standard extensions, including event packages, may go through any appropriate RAI working group. Informational header fields pass through Expert Review.
sections.eli5: Some names in the official lists need a full vote, and some only need one expert to say yes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC observes that complex, indeterminate protocol behavior that depends on many optional extensions is a fine breeding ground for security flaws. Every Internet-Draft presenting new requirements for SIP must discuss security requirements and implications. Every RFC that modifies or extends SIP must show adequate security, consider feature interactions, and not worsen SIP's existing security considerations.
sections.eli5: Every new SIP idea has to show it will not open a new door for troublemakers.

items.title: To SIPCORE
items.text: The requirements justify a change to core SIP, RFCs 3261 through 3265.

items.title: New effort
items.text: No core SIP change, but a new working group, BoF or similar is needed in RAI.

items.title: Existing work
items.text: The requirements fall within existing chartered RAI work.

items.title: Not now
items.text: The proposal should not be acted upon at this time.
